examMarks.basis: Chapter 1 questions in the 2022, 2023 and 2025 papers: 9, 9 and 9 marks (MCQ 2 + 3-mark + 4-mark each year)

stops.title: Chain rule for composite functions
stops.inShort: If y = f(u) and u = g(x) are both differentiable, then y is a differentiable function of x and dy/dx = (dy/du)·(du/dx). Differentiate the outer function first, keep the inside unchanged, then multiply by the derivative of the inside.

cards.text: A composite (function of a function) has one function sitting inside another, e.g. sin(log x) or e^{tan x}. Writing y = f[g(x)], g is the inner function and f is the outer function.

If y = f(u) is differentiable in u and u = g(x) is differentiable in x, then dy/dx = (dy/du)·(du/dx). In function notation: d/dx f[g(x)] = f '[g(x)]·g '(x). The proof uses δy/δx = (δy/δu)·(δu/δx) and the fact that δu → 0 as δx → 0 because u is continuous.
The rule extends to any number of links: if y = f(v), v = g(u), u = h(x) then dy/dx = (dy/dv)·(dv/du)·(du/dx). Peel the layers from outside to inside, multiplying one derivative per layer.

checks.q: If y = sin(log x), then dy/dx equals
checks.hint: Outer function sin, inner function log x.
checks.explain: dy/dx = cos(log x)·d/dx(log x) = cos(log x)/x.

checks.q: For y = e^{tan x}, the chain rule gives dy/dx = e^{tan x}·sec²x.
checks.hint: Derivative of e^{u} is e^{u}·du/dx.
checks.explain: True. The outer function e^{u} differentiates to itself; multiply by d/dx(tan x) = sec²x.

checks.hint: Apply the chain rule layer by layer: F'(x) = 15·G'{3G[5G(x)]}·G'[5G(x)]·G'(x).
checks.explain: Since G(0) = 0, every inner argument becomes 0 at x = 0, so F'(0) = 15·G'(0)·G'(0)·G'(0) = 15 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 405.

stops.title: Standard composite derivatives and value tables
sections: 1.1.3 Derivatives of some standard Composite Functions
stops.inShort: Table 1.1.2 lists ready results such as d/dx [f(x)]^{n} = n[f(x)]^{n−1}·f '(x), d/dx √f(x) = f '(x)/(2√f(x)), d/dx log f(x) = f '(x)/f(x) and d/dx a^{f(x)} = a^{f(x)}·log a·f '(x). Value-table questions just substitute the given f, g, f ', g ' values into the chain rule.

cards.text: d/dx log f(x) = f '(x)/f(x); d/dx e^{f(x)} = e^{f(x)}·f '(x); d/dx a^{f(x)} = a^{f(x)}·log a·f '(x). Simplify logs first: log[tan³x·sin⁴x] = 3 log tan x + 4 log sin x makes differentiation much shorter.
When only values are given, write the chain rule first, then substitute. For r(x) = f[g(x)], r '(a) = f '[g(a)]·g '(a): find g(a) in the table, read f ' at that new input, then multiply by g '(a).

checks.q: d/dx log[cos(x³ − 5)] equals
checks.hint: Use d/dx log f = f '/f, then the chain rule on cos.
checks.explain: d/dx log[cos(x³ − 5)] = [−sin(x³ − 5)·3x²]/cos(x³ − 5) = −3x² tan(x³ − 5).

checks.q: If f(x) = √(7g(x) − 3), g(3) = 4 and g'(3) = 5, find f '(3). (Enter as a decimal.)
d/dx [5^{sin x}] = 5^{sin x}·cos x.
checks.hint: Do not forget the log a factor for a^{f(x)}.
checks.explain: False. d/dx a^{f(x)} = a^{f(x)}·log a·f '(x), so the correct derivative is 5^{sin x}·log 5·cos x.

stops.title: Slope meaning and derivative of an inverse function
stops.inShort: f '(a) is the slope of the tangent to y = f(x) at x = a (limit of secant slopes). If y = f(x) has an inverse x = f^{−1}(y), then dx/dy = 1/(dy/dx), provided dy/dx ≠ 0. To find (f^{−1})'(b): solve f(a) = b, then (f^{−1})'(b) = 1/f '(a).

cards.text: The secant through P(a, f(a)) and Q(a + h, f(a + h)) has slope [f(a + h) − f(a)]/h. As h → 0, Q slides to P and the secant becomes the tangent, so slope of tangent at P = f '(a). Example: for y = x² + 3x + 2, dy/dx = 2x + 3, so the tangent at x = 2 has slope 2(2) + 3 = 7.

If y = f(x) is differentiable with dy/dx ≠ 0 and x = f^{−1}(y) exists, then x is a differentiable function of y and dx/dy = 1/(dy/dx). Alternative proof: differentiate f^{−1}[f(x)] = x by the chain rule to get (f^{−1})'[f(x)]·f '(x) = 1.

To find (f^{−1})'(b) you need the x for which f(x) = b, not x = b. Example: f(x) = x⁵ + 2x − 3 gives f(x) = −3 at x = 0, so (f^{−1})'(−3) = 1/f '(0) = 1/2. In general g '(x) = 1/f '[g(x)] when g = f^{−1}.

checks.q: If y = log x, the derivative found through its inverse x = e^{y} is
checks.hint: dy/dx = 1/(dx/dy).
checks.explain: x = e^{y} gives dx/dy = e^{y}, so dy/dx = 1/e^{y} = 1/x.

checks.hint: First solve f(x) = 0 to find which x maps to 0.
checks.explain: False. f(1) = 0, so (f^{−1})'(0) = 1/f '(1) = 1/(3 + 1) = 1/4. Using f '(0) is the classic trap.

checks.q: For y = 2x³ − 6x, the derivative of the inverse function at x = −2 is dx/dy = 1/k. Find k.
checks.hint: dx/dy = 1/(dy/dx) and dy/dx = 6x² − 6.
checks.explain: dy/dx = 6(−2)² − 6 = 18 at x = −2, so dx/dy = 1/18 and k = 18.

stops.title: Derivatives of inverse trigonometric functions
sections: 1.2.4 Derivatives of Standard Inverse trigonometric Functions
stops.inShort: d/dx sin^{−1}x = 1/√(1 − x²), d/dx cos^{−1}x = −1/√(1 − x²) (|x| < 1); d/dx tan^{−1}x = 1/(1 + x²), d/dx cot^{−1}x = −1/(1 + x²); d/dx sec^{−1}x = 1/(x√(x² − 1)), d/dx cosec^{−1}x = −1/(x√(x² − 1)) for x > 1. The 'co-' functions carry a minus sign.

cards.text: For y = sin^{−1}x write x = sin y, so dx/dy = cos y = √(1 − sin²y) = √(1 − x²) (positive because −π/2 ≤ y ≤ π/2). Then dy/dx = 1/√(1 − x²). The same 'invert, differentiate, reciprocate' idea proves every row of Table 1.2.1.

cos^{−1}, cot^{−1} and cosec^{−1} have derivatives that are the negatives of sin^{−1}, tan^{−1} and sec^{−1}. That is why sin^{−1}x + cos^{−1}x, tan^{−1}x + cot^{−1}x and sec^{−1}x + cosec^{−1}x each have derivative 0 and equal the constant π/2.
Combine with the chain rule: d/dx sin^{−1}[f(x)] = f '(x)/√(1 − [f(x)]²), d/dx tan^{−1}[f(x)] = f '(x)/(1 + [f(x)]²), and so on (Table 1.2.2). Example: d/dx sin^{−1}(x³) = 3x²/√(1 − x⁶).

checks.q: d/dx tan^{−1}(log x) equals
checks.hint: Chain rule: f(x) = log x, f '(x) = 1/x.
checks.explain: d/dx tan^{−1}(log x) = (1/x)/(1 + (log x)²) = 1/[x(1 + (log x)²)].

checks.q: The derivative of sec^{−1}x is negative for x > 1.
checks.hint: Look at the sign in Table 1.2.1 and Note 2 on p. 19.
checks.explain: False. d/dx sec^{−1}x = 1/(x√(x² − 1)) > 0 for x > 1; the graph of sec^{−1}x is increasing. It is cosec^{−1}x whose derivative is negative.

checks.q: Using derivatives, why is sin^{−1}x + cos^{−1}x constant on (−1, 1)?
options: Because sin and cos are complementary
checks.hint: A function whose derivative is zero everywhere on an interval is constant.
checks.explain: f '(x) = 0, so f is constant; putting x = 0 gives f(0) = 0 + π/2, hence the constant is π/2.

stops.title: Simplifying inverse trig by substitution
stops.inShort: Before differentiating messy inverse-trig expressions, substitute to simplify: √(1 − x²) → x = sin θ or cos θ; 2x/(1 + x²), (1 − x²)/(1 + x²), 2x/(1 − x²) → x = tan θ; 3x − 4x³ → x = sin θ; (1 − cos x)/(1 + cos x) → use half-angle identities. Then use sin^{−1}(sin θ) = θ and differentiate the simple result.

cards.text: Expressions like sin^{−1}(2x√(1 − x²)) are painful by the chain rule. With x = sin θ the inside becomes sin 2θ, so y = 2θ = 2 sin^{−1}x and dy/dx = 2/√(1 − x²) in one line (for |x| < 1/√2).

sin 2θ = 2 tan θ/(1 + tan²θ), cos 2θ = (1 − tan²θ)/(1 + tan²θ), tan 2θ = 2 tan θ/(1 − tan²θ), sin 3θ = 3 sin θ − 4 sin³θ, cos 3θ = 4 cos³θ − 3 cos θ, 1 + cos x = 2cos²(x/2), 1 − cos x = 2sin²(x/2), sin x = 2 sin(x/2) cos(x/2).
sin^{−1}(cos θ) = π/2 − θ and tan^{−1}(cot θ) = π/2 − θ (Table 1.2.3). These turn cos^{−1} into sin^{−1} and cot into tan before simplifying. Remember the constant π/2 disappears on differentiation.

checks.q: If y = tan^{−1}[2x/(1 − x²)] for |x| < 1, then dy/dx =
checks.hint: Put x = tan θ.
checks.explain: x = tan θ gives 2x/(1 − x²) = tan 2θ, so y = 2θ = 2 tan^{−1}x and dy/dx = 2/(1 + x²).

checks.q: Which substitution simplifies cos^{−1}[(1 − x²)/(1 + x²)]?
checks.hint: Recall the identity for cos 2θ in terms of tan θ.
checks.explain: With x = tan θ, (1 − tan²θ)/(1 + tan²θ) = cos 2θ, so y = 2θ = 2 tan^{−1}x (for x ≥ 0) and dy/dx = 2/(1 + x²).

checks.q: For y = tan^{−1}[(1 − cos x)/sin x], 0 < x < π, which line is the correct simplification?
checks.hint: Write 1 − cos x = 2 sin²(x/2) and sin x = 2 sin(x/2) cos(x/2).
checks.explain: (1 − cos x)/sin x = 2sin²(x/2)/[2 sin(x/2) cos(x/2)] = tan(x/2), so y = x/2 and dy/dx = 1/2.

stops.title: Logarithmic differentiation
stops.inShort: Take log on both sides when y is a variable power [f(x)]^{g(x)} or a big product/quotient. Then log y = g(x)·log f(x), differentiate implicitly: (1/y)·dy/dx = ..., and multiply back by y. Shortcut: d/dx f^{g} = f^{g}[g·f '/f + log f·g'].

cards.text: Use logarithmic differentiation for (i) functions like x^{x}, (sin x)^{x}, x^{tan x}, where both base and power vary, and (ii) long products/quotients/roots such as (x + 1)²/[(x + 2)³(x + 3)⁴], where logs turn products into sums.
Step 1: y = [f(x)]^{g(x)} ⇒ log y = g(x) log f(x). Step 2: differentiate: (1/y)(dy/dx) = g(x)·f '(x)/f(x) + log f(x)·g '(x). Step 3: dy/dx = y[ ... ], and replace y by the original function.
For y = x^{x} + (sin x)^{x} you cannot take log of the whole sum usefully. Put u = x^{x}, v = (sin x)^{x}, find du/dx and dv/dx separately by logs, then dy/dx = du/dx + dv/dx.

checks.q: If y = x^{x}, then dy/dx =
checks.hint: log y = x log x.
checks.explain: (1/y) dy/dx = log x + x·(1/x) = 1 + log x, so dy/dx = x^{x}(1 + log x).

checks.q: To differentiate y = x^{sin x} + (log x)^{x}, it is best to take log of both sides of the whole equation at once.
checks.hint: log(u + v) does not split.
checks.explain: False. log(u + v) ≠ log u + log v, so treat u = x^{sin x} and v = (log x)^{x} separately and add their derivatives.

checks.q: If log y = tan x·log x, then (1/y)·dy/dx =
checks.hint: Product rule on tan x·log x.
checks.explain: d/dx(tan x·log x) = tan x·(1/x) + log x·sec²x.

stops.title: Implicit functions
stops.inShort: When x and y are mixed in one equation (e.g. x³ + y³ = 3axy), differentiate every term w.r.t. x, treating y as a function of x so that d/dx(y^{n}) = n y^{n−1}·dy/dx. Collect all dy/dx terms on one side and solve. Taking logs first often helps (e.g. x^{y} = e^{x−y}).

cards.text: y = x² + 3 is explicit (y alone on one side). x² + xy + y² = 7 is implicit: y cannot easily be isolated. We still find dy/dx by differentiating both sides directly.
Every y-term picks up a factor dy/dx: d/dx(y²) = 2y·y', d/dx(sin y) = cos y·y', d/dx(xy) = x·y' + y (product rule), d/dx(e^{y}) = e^{y}·y'.

For x^{y} = e^{x − y}, take log: y log x = x − y ⇒ y = x/(1 + log x), then differentiate explicitly. For y'(a) questions, first find y at x = a from the original equation, then substitute both into the differentiated equation.

checks.q: If x² + y² = 25, then dy/dx =
checks.hint: Differentiate: 2x + 2y·y' = 0.

checks.q: d/dx (xy) = y·dy/dx.
checks.hint: xy is a product of two functions of x.
checks.explain: False. By the product rule d/dx(xy) = x·dy/dx + y.

checks.q: If e^{x} + e^{y} = e^{x + y}, then dy/dx =
checks.hint: Differentiate, then use e^{x + y} = e^{x} + e^{y} to simplify.
checks.explain: e^{x} + e^{y}y' = e^{x+y}(1 + y'). Solving and simplifying with e^{x + y} = e^{x} + e^{y} gives dy/dx = −e^{y − x}.

stops.title: Special implicit forms and infinite expressions
stops.inShort: x^{m}y^{n} = (x + y)^{m+n} always gives dy/dx = y/x (and d²y/dx² = 0). If any function of (x^{n} − y^{n})/(x^{n} + y^{n}) equals a constant, that fraction itself is a constant, so y^{n} = c·x^{n}. For an infinite radical y = √(f(x) + y), square to get y² = f(x) + y and differentiate.

cards.text: Take log of x^{m}y^{n} = (x + y)^{m+n}: m log x + n log y = (m + n) log(x + y). Differentiating and collecting dy/dx terms produces the same factor (nx − my) on both sides; cancelling it leaves dy/dx = y/x. Board examiners expect you to show the working, not just quote the result.

If f[(x^{n} − y^{n})/(x^{n} + y^{n})] = constant, then (x^{n} − y^{n})/(x^{n} + y^{n}) = k (a constant). Cross-multiply and use componendo-dividendo to get y^{n} = c·x^{n}, then differentiate: dy/dx = (y/x) or a multiple like 99x²/(101y²).
If y = √(tan x + √(tan x + √(tan x + ... ∞))), the tail after the first term is y itself, so y = √(tan x + y) ⇒ y² = tan x + y. Then 2y y' = sec²x + y' ⇒ dy/dx = sec²x/(2y − 1).

checks.q: If x⁷y⁵ = (x + y)^{12}, then dy/dx =
checks.hint: Here m = 7, n = 5 and m + n = 12.
checks.explain: This is the form x^{m}y^{n} = (x + y)^{m+n}, which gives dy/dx = y/x.

checks.q: If y = √(cos x + √(cos x + √(cos x + ... ∞))), then dy/dx =
checks.hint: y² = cos x + y; differentiate both sides.
checks.explain: 2y y' = −sin x + y' ⇒ y'(2y − 1) = −sin x ⇒ y' = sin x/(1 − 2y).

checks.q: For an implicit relation x^{m}y^{n} = (x + y)^{m+n}, the second derivative d²y/dx² is 0.
checks.hint: If dy/dx = y/x, then y/x is constant.
checks.explain: True. dy/dx = y/x means y = cx (a straight line through the origin), so d²y/dx² = 0 (Let us Remember, p. 61).

stops.title: Derivatives of parametric functions
stops.inShort: If x = f(t) and y = g(t) are differentiable and dx/dt ≠ 0, then dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt). Differentiate x and y separately w.r.t. the parameter, then divide. This theorem with its proof is a regular 4-mark board question.

cards.text: Sometimes x and y are both given in terms of a third variable t (or θ) called a parameter, e.g. x = at², y = 2at (a parabola) or x = a cos θ, y = b sin θ (an ellipse).

Give t an increment δt; x and y change by δx and δy. Then δy/δx = (δy/δt)/(δx/δt). As δt → 0, δx → 0 and δy → 0 (x and y are continuous), so taking limits gives dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt), provided dx/dt ≠ 0.
To find dy/dx at θ = π/6 etc., first get the general expression in t or θ, then substitute the parameter value. Example: x = at², y = 2at gives dy/dx = 2a/(2at) = 1/t.

checks.q: If x = a cos θ, y = b sin θ, then dy/dx =
checks.hint: dx/dθ = −a sin θ, dy/dθ = b cos θ.
checks.explain: dy/dx = b cos θ/(−a sin θ) = −(b/a) cot θ.

checks.q: If x = at², y = 2at, find dy/dx at t = 2. (Enter as a decimal.)
checks.hint: dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt).
checks.explain: dy/dt = 2a, dx/dt = 2at, so dy/dx = 1/t = 1/2 = 0.5 at t = 2.

checks.q: In the parametric theorem, the condition dx/dt ≠ 0 is needed because dx/dt appears in the denominator.
checks.hint: Look at the formula's denominator.
checks.explain: True. dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) is undefined if dx/dt = 0 (tangent is vertical there).

stops.title: Derivative of one function with respect to another
sections: 1.4.3 Differentiation of one function with respect to another function
stops.inShort: To differentiate u = f(x) w.r.t. v = g(x), treat x as the parameter: du/dv = (du/dx)/(dv/dx), with dv/dx ≠ 0. For inverse-trig pairs, simplify both u and v by the same substitution first — the answer is often a constant.

cards.text: If u = f(x) and v = g(x) are differentiable and dv/dx ≠ 0, then du/dv = (du/dx)/(dv/dx). This is just the parametric theorem with x playing the role of the parameter.
Derivative of 7^{x} w.r.t. x⁷: u = 7^{x} gives du/dx = 7^{x} log 7; v = x⁷ gives dv/dx = 7x⁶. So du/dv = 7^{x} log 7/(7x⁶).
Differentiate tan^{−1}[2x/(1 − x²)] w.r.t. sin^{−1}[2x/(1 + x²)]: with x = tan θ, u = 2θ and v = 2θ (for |x| < 1), so du/dv = 1. Always state the range of x for which the simplification holds.

checks.q: The derivative of sin²x w.r.t. cos²x is
checks.hint: du/dx = 2 sin x cos x, dv/dx = −2 cos x sin x.
checks.explain: du/dv = (2 sin x cos x)/(−2 sin x cos x) = −1. (Also: sin²x = 1 − cos²x.)

checks.q: The derivative of x^{x} w.r.t. x is x^{x}(1 + log x). Hence the derivative of x^{x} w.r.t. log x is
checks.hint: Divide by d/dx(log x) = 1/x.
checks.explain: du/dv = x^{x}(1 + log x)/(1/x) = x^{x+1}(1 + log x).

checks.q: To differentiate f(x) w.r.t. g(x), you compute f '(x)·g '(x).
checks.hint: It is a quotient, not a product.
checks.explain: False. The derivative of f w.r.t. g is f '(x)/g '(x), provided g '(x) ≠ 0.

stops.title: Second order derivatives
stops.inShort: d²y/dx² = d/dx(dy/dx), also written y'' or y₂. For parametric curves, d²y/dx² = d/dt(dy/dx) ÷ (dx/dt) — never (d²y/dt²)/(d²x/dt²). 'Show that (1 − x²)y₂ − xy₁ + m²y = 0' type questions: get y₁, clear the root/denominator, square if needed, then differentiate again.

cards.text: If y = f(x), then y₁ = dy/dx = f '(x), y₂ = d²y/dx² = f ''(x), y₃ = d³y/dx³, ..., y_{n} = dⁿy/dxⁿ = f^{(n)}(x). Each is the derivative of the previous one.

For x = f(t), y = g(t): first find dy/dx as a function of t. Then d²y/dx² = [d/dt(dy/dx)]·(dt/dx) = [d/dt(dy/dx)]/(dx/dt). Example: x = at², y = 2at ⇒ dy/dx = 1/t ⇒ d²y/dx² = (−1/t²)/(2at) = −1/(2at³).

For y = e^{m tan⁻¹x}: y₁ = my/(1 + x²) ⇒ (1 + x²)y₁ = my. Differentiate again with the product rule: (1 + x²)y₂ + 2xy₁ = my₁. Clearing denominators before the second differentiation keeps the algebra short.

checks.q: If y = x³ log x, then d²y/dx² =
checks.hint: y₁ = 3x² log x + x².
checks.explain: y₁ = 3x² log x + x², so y₂ = 6x log x + 3x + 2x = x(5 + 6 log x).

checks.q: For x = at², y = 2at, d²y/dx² = (d²y/dt²)/(d²x/dt²) = 0/(2a) = 0.
checks.hint: The correct method is d/dt(dy/dx) divided by dx/dt.
checks.explain: False. dy/dx = 1/t, so d²y/dx² = (−1/t²)/(2at) = −1/(2at³), which is not 0.

checks.q: If ax² + 2hxy + by² = 0, then d²y/dx² equals
checks.hint: This homogeneous equation represents a pair of lines through the origin, so dy/dx = y/x.
checks.explain: Differentiating gives dy/dx = y/x; then d²y/dx² = (x·y' − y)/x² = (x·(y/x) − y)/x² = 0.

stops.title: nth order derivatives and the miscellaneous exercise
stops.inShort: For the nth derivative: find y₁, y₂, y₃, spot the pattern in coefficients, powers and signs, then write y_{n}. Key results: (ax + b)^{−1} → (−1)ⁿ n! aⁿ/(ax + b)^{n+1}; log(ax + b) → (−1)^{n−1}(n − 1)! aⁿ/(ax + b)ⁿ; sin(ax + b) → aⁿ sin(ax + b + nπ/2); e^{ax+b} → aⁿ e^{ax+b}.

cards.text: Step 1: differentiate 3 times. Step 2: observe how the coefficient, angle, power and sign change. Step 3: write the nth derivative from the pattern. Textbook uses (−1)ⁿ for alternating signs and n! for growing products.
y = 1/(ax + b): y₁ = −a/(ax + b)², y₂ = 2a²/(ax + b)³, y₃ = −6a³/(ax + b)⁴ ⇒ y_{n} = (−1)ⁿ n! aⁿ/(ax + b)^{n+1}. Since log x has first derivative 1/x, y = log x gives y_{n} = (−1)^{n−1}(n − 1)!/xⁿ.

Each derivative of sin x shifts the angle by π/2: d/dx sin x = cos x = sin(x + π/2). Hence dⁿ/dxⁿ sin(ax + b) = aⁿ sin(ax + b + nπ/2) and dⁿ/dxⁿ cos(ax + b) = aⁿ cos(ax + b + nπ/2). For e^{ax} sin(bx + c), write a = r cos α, b = r sin α to get rⁿ e^{ax} sin(bx + c + nα).

checks.q: The nth derivative of e^{3x + 2} is
checks.hint: Each differentiation multiplies by 3.

checks.q: The nth derivative of log x is
checks.hint: Start from y₁ = 1/x and apply the 1/x pattern n − 1 more times.

checks.q: dⁿ/dxⁿ (cos x) = cos(x + nπ/2).
checks.hint: Each derivative of cos x is cos shifted by π/2.
checks.explain: True. d/dx cos x = −sin x = cos(x + π/2); repeating n times adds nπ/2 to the angle.

board.text: Let f(1) = 3, f '(1) = −1/3, g(1) = −4 and g '(1) = −8/3. The derivative of √([f(x)]² + [g(x)]²) w.r.t. x at x = 1 is ______.

points.text: Chain rule: h '(x) = [f f ' + g g ']/√(f² + g²); substitute to get (29/3)/5; Write the correct option with letter: (d) 29/15

board.text: Find the nth order derivative of log x.
board.answer: Let y = log x. Then y₁ = 1/x = x^{−1}, y₂ = (−1)x^{−2} = −1/x², y₃ = (−1)(−2)x^{−3} = 2!/x³, y₄ = (−1)(−2)(−3)x^{−4} = −3!/x⁴. Observing the pattern (sign alternates starting with +, coefficient (n − 1)!, power of x is n): dⁿy/dxⁿ = (−1)^{n−1}(n − 1)!/xⁿ.

points.text: Find y₁ = 1/x, y₂ = −1/x², y₃ = 2!/x³ (at least three derivatives)
Identify the pattern of signs, factorial coefficient and powers
Conclude dⁿy/dxⁿ = (−1)^{n−1}(n − 1)!/xⁿ

board.text: If x = f(t) and y = g(t) are differentiable functions of t so that y is a function of x and if dx/dt ≠ 0, then prove that dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt). Hence find the derivative of 7^{x} w.r.t. x⁷.
board.answer: Proof: Let δt be a small increment in t, and δx, δy the corresponding increments in x and y (δt, δx, δy ≠ 0). Then δy/δx = (δy/δt)/(δx/δt). Since x and y are differentiable (hence continuous) functions of t, δx → 0 and δy → 0 as δt → 0. Taking limits, lim_{δx→0} δy/δx = [lim_{δt→0} δy/δt]/[lim_{δt→0} δx/δt] = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt). As dy/dt and dx/dt exist and dx/dt ≠ 0, the right side is finite, so dy/dx exists and dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt). Hence: let u = 7^{x} and v = x⁷. du/dx = 7^{x} log 7, dv/dx = 7x⁶. Treating x as the parameter, du/dv = (du/dx)/(dv/dx) = 7^{x} log 7/(7x⁶) = 7^{x−1} log 7/x⁶.

points.text: Take increments δt, δx, δy and write δy/δx = (δy/δt)/(δx/δt)
Use continuity: δx → 0, δy → 0 as δt → 0 and take limits
Conclude dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) with dx/dt ≠ 0
Hence: du/dv = 7^{x} log 7/(7x⁶)

board.text: If y is a function of x and log(x + y) = 2xy, then the value of y'(0) = ______.
board.answer: (d) 1. At x = 0: log(0 + y) = 0 ⇒ y = 1. Differentiating implicitly: (1 + y')/(x + y) = 2y + 2xy'. At (0, 1): (1 + y')/1 = 2(1) + 0 ⇒ y'(0) = 1.

points.text: Find y = 1 at x = 0 and differentiate: (1 + y')/(x + y) = 2y + 2xy'; Substitute (0, 1) to get y'(0) = 1 and write option (d) 1

board.text: If y = √(tan x + √(tan x + √(tan x + ... + ∞))), then show that dy/dx = sec²x/(2y − 1). Find dy/dx at x = 0.
board.answer: Since the expression continues to infinity, y = √(tan x + y). Squaring: y² = tan x + y. Differentiating w.r.t. x: 2y·dy/dx = sec²x + dy/dx ⇒ (2y − 1)·dy/dx = sec²x ⇒ dy/dx = sec²x/(2y − 1). At x = 0: y² = 0 + y ⇒ y = 1 (taking the non-zero value of the infinite expression). Hence dy/dx at x = 0 is sec²0/(2(1) − 1) = 1/1 = 1.

points.text: Write y = √(tan x + y), i.e. y² = tan x + y
Differentiate and solve: dy/dx = sec²x/(2y − 1)
At x = 0, y = 1, so dy/dx = 1

board.text: If y = cos(m cos^{−1}x), then show that (1 − x²)·d²y/dx² − x·dy/dx + m²y = 0.
board.answer: y = cos(m cos^{−1}x). Differentiating: dy/dx = −sin(m cos^{−1}x)·m·(−1/√(1 − x²)) = m sin(m cos^{−1}x)/√(1 − x²). So √(1 − x²)·dy/dx = m sin(m cos^{−1}x). Squaring: (1 − x²)(dy/dx)² = m² sin²(m cos^{−1}x) = m²[1 − cos²(m cos^{−1}x)] = m²(1 − y²). Differentiating again: (1 − x²)·2(dy/dx)(d²y/dx²) + (dy/dx)²(−2x) = m²(−2y·dy/dx). Dividing throughout by 2·dy/dx: (1 − x²)·d²y/dx² − x·dy/dx = −m²y, i.e. (1 − x²)·d²y/dx² − x·dy/dx + m²y = 0.

points.text: First derivative: dy/dx = m sin(m cos^{−1}x)/√(1 − x²)
Square to get (1 − x²)(dy/dx)² = m²(1 − y²)
Differentiate again using product and chain rules
Divide by 2·dy/dx and arrange to the required result
Note f(0) = −3 and use (f^{−1})'(−3) = 1/f '(0) with f '(x) = 5x⁴ + 2; Write the correct option with letter: (d) 1/2

board.text: If y = e^{m tan^{−1}x}, then show that (1 + x²)·d²y/dx² + (2x − m)·dy/dx = 0.
board.answer: y = e^{m tan^{−1}x}. Differentiating: dy/dx = e^{m tan^{−1}x}·m/(1 + x²) = my/(1 + x²). So (1 + x²)·dy/dx = my. Differentiating again: (1 + x²)·d²y/dx² + 2x·dy/dx = m·dy/dx. Hence (1 + x²)·d²y/dx² + (2x − m)·dy/dx = 0.

points.text: dy/dx = my/(1 + x²), i.e. (1 + x²)·dy/dx = my
Differentiate again: (1 + x²)y₂ + 2xy₁ = my₁
Rearrange to (1 + x²)y₂ + (2x − m)y₁ = 0

board.text: If x = f(t) and y = g(t) are differentiable functions of t so that y is a differentiable function of x and dx/dt ≠ 0, then prove that dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt). Hence find dy/dx if x = sin t and y = cos t.
board.answer: Proof: Let δt be a small increment in t with corresponding increments δx and δy in x and y (all non-zero). Then δy/δx = (δy/δt)/(δx/δt). As x and y are differentiable, they are continuous, so δx → 0 and δy → 0 as δt → 0. Taking limits: dy/dx = lim_{δx→0} δy/δx = [lim_{δt→0} δy/δt]/[lim_{δt→0} δx/δt] = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt), which is finite because dx/dt ≠ 0. Hence: x = sin t ⇒ dx/dt = cos t; y = cos t ⇒ dy/dt = −sin t. Therefore dy/dx = −sin t/cos t = −tan t.

points.text: Take increments δt, δx, δy and write δy/δx = (δy/δt)/(δx/δt)
Use continuity: δx → 0, δy → 0 as δt → 0 and take limits
Conclude dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) with dx/dt ≠ 0
Hence: dx/dt = cos t, dy/dt = −sin t, so dy/dx = −tan t

board.text: A table of values is given — at x = 2: f = 1, g = 6, f ' = −3, g ' = 4; at x = 4: f = 3, g = 4, f ' = 5, g ' = −6; at x = 6: f = 5, g = 2, f ' = −4, g ' = 7. (i) If r(x) = f[g(x)], find r '(2). (ii) If R(x) = g[3 + f(x)], find R '(4). (iii) If s(x) = f[9 − f(x)], find s '(4). (iv) If S(x) = g[g(x)], find S '(6).
Using derivative, prove that tan^{−1}x + cot^{−1}x = π/2.
board.answer: Let f(x) = tan^{−1}x + cot^{−1}x. Then f '(x) = 1/(1 + x²) − 1/(1 + x²) = 0 for all x ∈ R, so f(x) is a constant, say c. Putting x = 0: c = f(0) = tan^{−1}0 + cot^{−1}0 = 0 + π/2 = π/2. Hence tan^{−1}x + cot^{−1}x = π/2.

points.text: Differentiate: f '(x) = 1/(1 + x²) − 1/(1 + x²) = 0, so f is constant
Evaluate at x = 0 to get the constant π/2

board.text: If y = sec(tan^{−1}x), then dy/dx at x = 1 is equal to:
board.answer: (c) 1/√2. dy/dx = sec(tan^{−1}x)·tan(tan^{−1}x)·1/(1 + x²) = sec(tan^{−1}x)·x/(1 + x²). At x = 1: sec(π/4)·1/2 = √2/2 = 1/√2. (Alternatively y = √(1 + x²), so dy/dx = x/√(1 + x²) = 1/√2 at x = 1.)

points.text: Differentiate with the chain rule and substitute x = 1: sec(π/4)·(1/2); Write the correct option with letter: (c) 1/√2

board.text: Differentiate sin^{−1}(2x√(1 − x²)) w.r.t. x, for |x| < 1/√2.
board.answer: Let y = sin^{−1}(2x√(1 − x²)). Put x = sin θ, so θ = sin^{−1}x; since |x| < 1/√2, −π/4 < θ < π/4 and −π/2 < 2θ < π/2. Then 2x√(1 − x²) = 2 sin θ cos θ = sin 2θ, so y = sin^{−1}(sin 2θ) = 2θ = 2 sin^{−1}x. Differentiating: dy/dx = 2/√(1 − x²).

points.text: Substitute x = sin θ and simplify to sin 2θ
Use the range to write y = 2θ = 2 sin^{−1}x
Differentiate: dy/dx = 2/√(1 − x²)

board.answer: Let y = x^{tan x}. Taking log: log y = tan x·log x. Differentiating w.r.t. x: (1/y)·dy/dx = tan x·(1/x) + log x·sec²x. Therefore dy/dx = x^{tan x}[tan x/x + sec²x·log x].

points.text: Take logarithm: log y = tan x·log x
Differentiate using product rule: (1/y)y' = tan x/x + sec²x log x
Final: dy/dx = x^{tan x}[tan x/x + sec²x log x]

board.text: If x^{y} = e^{x − y}, then show that dy/dx = log x/(1 + log x)².
board.answer: Taking log on both sides: y log x = (x − y) log e = x − y. So y(1 + log x) = x, i.e. y = x/(1 + log x). Differentiating by the quotient rule: dy/dx = [(1 + log x)·1 − x·(1/x)]/(1 + log x)² = (1 + log x − 1)/(1 + log x)² = log x/(1 + log x)².

points.text: Take log: y log x = x − y
Express y = x/(1 + log x)
Quotient rule to get dy/dx = log x/(1 + log x)²

board.text: If x⁷·y⁵ = (x + y)^{12}, show that dy/dx = y/x.
board.answer: Taking log: 7 log x + 5 log y = 12 log(x + y). Differentiating: 7/x + (5/y)·dy/dx = [12/(x + y)]·(1 + dy/dx). So dy/dx·[5/y − 12/(x + y)] = 12/(x + y) − 7/x, i.e. dy/dx·(5x + 5y − 12y)/[y(x + y)] = (12x − 7x − 7y)/[x(x + y)], i.e. dy/dx·(5x − 7y)/[y(x + y)] = (5x − 7y)/[x(x + y)]. Cancelling (5x − 7y)/(x + y): dy/dx = y/x.

points.text: Take log and differentiate: 7/x + (5/y)y' = 12(1 + y')/(x + y)
Collect y' terms: y'(5x − 7y)/[y(x + y)] = (5x − 7y)/[x(x + y)]
Cancel common factor to get dy/dx = y/x

board.text: Find d²y/dx² if x = a(θ − sin θ), y = a(1 − cos θ).
board.answer: dx/dθ = a(1 − cos θ) = 2a sin²(θ/2); dy/dθ = a sin θ = 2a sin(θ/2)cos(θ/2). So dy/dx = cot(θ/2). Then d²y/dx² = d/dθ[cot(θ/2)]·dθ/dx = −(1/2)cosec²(θ/2)·1/(2a sin²(θ/2)) = −1/(4a sin⁴(θ/2)) = −(1/4a)cosec⁴(θ/2).

points.text: dx/dθ = 2a sin²(θ/2), dy/dθ = 2a sin(θ/2)cos(θ/2), so dy/dx = cot(θ/2)
Differentiate w.r.t. θ and multiply by dθ/dx
Simplify: d²y/dx² = −(1/4a)cosec⁴(θ/2)
Compute y₁, y₂, y₃ with the chain-rule factor 3 each time
Identify the pattern (−1)ⁿ, n!, 3ⁿ and power n + 1
Conclude dⁿy/dxⁿ = (−1)ⁿ n! 3ⁿ/(3x − 5)^{n+1}

derivations.title: Prove the chain rule dy/dx = (dy/du)·(du/dx)
derivations.given: y = f(u) is a differentiable function of u and u = g(x) is a differentiable function of x (u not constant). Prove y is a differentiable function of x and dy/dx = (dy/du)·(du/dx).

steps.line: Give x an increment δx; let δu, δy be the corresponding increments in u and y (all non-zero)
wrong: Give u an increment δu and keep x fixed
Assume δy = δx so that the ratio is 1
steps.note: Start every increment proof by naming all three increments.
Multiply and divide by δu; this is pure algebra.

steps.line: As δx → 0, δu → 0, because u = g(x) is differentiable and hence continuous
steps.note: Continuity is the key justification examiners look for.
Limit of a product is the product of limits.

steps.line: The right side exists and is finite, so dy/dx exists and dy/dx = (dy/du)·(du/dx)
steps.note: Conclude explicitly that y is differentiable in x.

derivations.title: Prove dx/dy = 1/(dy/dx) for an inverse function
derivations.given: y = f(x) is differentiable with dy/dx ≠ 0 and x = f^{−1}(y) exists. Prove x is a differentiable function of y and dx/dy = 1/(dy/dx).

steps.line: Let δx be an increment in x and δy the corresponding increment in y, with δx, δy ≠ 0
wrong: Let δy = 0 for a small increment δx
steps.note: Non-zero increments let us divide.
The two ratios are reciprocals.

steps.line: As δx → 0, δy → 0 (f is continuous), so lim_{δy→0} δx/δy = 1/lim_{δx→0} (δy/δx)
wrong: Take limits only on the left side
steps.note: Continuity of f links the two limits.

steps.line: Since dy/dx exists and is non-zero, dx/dy exists and dx/dy = 1/(dy/dx)
steps.note: The condition dy/dx ≠ 0 makes the reciprocal finite.

derivations.title: Prove d/dx (sin^{−1}x) = 1/√(1 − x²)
derivations.given: y = sin^{−1}x, −1 ≤ x ≤ 1, −π/2 ≤ y ≤ π/2. Prove dy/dx = 1/√(1 − x²) for |x| < 1.

steps.note: Rewrite the inverse function in direct form.
Differentiate w.r.t. y and use sin y = x.

steps.line: cos y > 0 for −π/2 < y < π/2, so dx/dy = √(1 − x²)
wrong: cos y < 0 in this range, so dx/dy = −√(1 − x²)
steps.note: The principal branch lies in quadrants I and IV where cosine is positive.
Use the inverse function theorem.

derivations.title: Logarithmic differentiation of [f(x)]^{g(x)}
derivations.given: Derive the shortcut d/dx [f(x)]^{g(x)} = f^{g}[g·f '/f + log f·g '], then apply it to y = (sin x)^{x}.

steps.line: y = f^{g} ⇒ log y = g·log f
steps.note: Take natural log of both sides; the power comes down.
Product rule on the right; chain rule gives (1/y)y' on the left.
Multiply by y and substitute y = f^{g}. Note: both the power-rule term and the exponential term appear.

steps.line: For y = (sin x)^{x}: dy/dx = (sin x)^{x}[x cot x + log(sin x)]
steps.note: Here f = sin x, g = x, f '/f = cot x, g ' = 1.

derivations.title: Show x^{m}y^{n} = (x + y)^{m+n} gives dy/dx = y/x
derivations.given: If x^{m}·y^{n} = (x + y)^{m+n}, prove that dy/dx = y/x.

steps.line: m log x + n log y = (m + n) log(x + y)
wrong: m log x · n log y = (m + n) log(x + y)
steps.note: Logs turn the product and powers into sums.
Differentiate; do not forget the chain-rule factor (1 + y') on the right.
Collect all y' terms on the left.
Simplify each side over a common denominator — the same factor nx − my appears.
Result is independent of m and n.

derivations.title: Prove dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) for parametric functions
derivations.given: x = f(t) and y = g(t) are differentiable functions of t, y is a function of x, and dx/dt ≠ 0. Prove dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt).

wrong: Let δx be an increment in x keeping t fixed

Divide numerator and denominator by δt.

steps.line: As δt → 0, δx → 0 and δy → 0, since x and y are differentiable, hence continuous, functions of t

wrong: lim δy/δx = lim δy/δt − lim δx/δt

derivations.given: If y = e^{m tan^{−1}x}, show that (1 + x²)·d²y/dx² + (2x − m)·dy/dx = 0.

Product rule on the left side.
Move m·dy/dx to the left.

derivations.given: If y = cos(m cos^{−1}x), show that (1 − x²)·d²y/dx² − x·dy/dx + m²y = 0.

Differentiate both sides; product rule on the left.
Every term had a common factor 2y₁.

derivations.title: nth derivative of log x
derivations.given: Find dⁿy/dxⁿ for y = log x.

steps.note: Standard derivative of log x.
Power rule each time; signs alternate.
Coefficient is (n − 1)! for the nth derivative.
Check: n = 1 gives +0!/x = 1/x ✓.

items.f: d/dx log f(x) = f '(x)/f(x); d/dx log_{a} f(x) = f '(x)/(f(x) log a)
d/dx e^{f(x)} = e^{f(x)}·f '(x); d/dx a^{f(x)} = a^{f(x)}·log a·f '(x)
d/dx sin f = cos f·f '; d/dx tan f = sec²f·f '; d/dx sec f = sec f tan f·f '

sin^{−1}x + cos^{−1}x = tan^{−1}x + cot^{−1}x = sec^{−1}x + cosec^{−1}x = π/2
